questions.title: What is React?
questions.summary: R^ is a declarative JavaScript library for building UI from reusable C^s.
questions.answer: R^ is a declarative, C^-based JavaScript library for building interactive UIs. You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and R^ coordinates updates when props or state change.
questions.underTheHood: R^ creates an element tree from C^ output, reconciles it against previous work, and commits necessary changes to the host environment. In the browser, React DOM handles DOM updates.
pitfalls: R^ is a UI library, not a complete framework.
R^ does not necessarily update the DOM on every re-r().
questions.recall: R^ → Declarative UI → C^ → State/Props → r() → Reconciliation → Commit.

questions.title: What is a Component?
questions.summary: A C^ is a reusable UI unit, commonly implemented as a F() returning R^ elements.
questions.answer: A C^ is an independent, reusable UI unit. A functional C^ receives props and returns R^ elements describing the UI. C^ composition builds complex interfaces from smaller pieces.
questions.underTheHood: R^ calls functional C^s during rendering and associates their H^ state with their position and identity in the R^ tree.
pitfalls: C^ names must start with uppercase letters.
Do not call H^-using C^s as ordinary F()s.
questions.recall: C^ = F(props) → R^ elements → reusable UI.

questions.title: What is JSX?
questions.summary: JSX is JavaScript syntax that describes R^ elements using HTML-like markup.
questions.answer: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that makes UI declarations readable. Build tools transform JSX into calls that create R^ element objects. JSX expressions use braces to embed JavaScript values.
questions.underTheHood: Modern JSX transforms commonly compile JSX into jsx()/jsxs() calls from react/jsx-runtime. The resulting elements are descriptions, not actual DOM nodes.
pitfalls: Return a single root element or Fragment.
JSX expressions cannot directly contain statements.

questions.title: React Elements vs Components
questions.summary: An element describes what to render; a C^ defines reusable logic that produces elements.
questions.answer: A R^ element is an immutable description of UI containing a type, props, and key. A C^ is a F() or class that defines how UI elements are produced.
questions.underTheHood: R^ uses element descriptions to build and update its Fiber tree. Elements are lightweight descriptions rather than mounted instances or DOM nodes.
pitfalls: An element is not a DOM node.
Creating an element does not immediately mount it.
questions.recall: C^ → produces Element → R^ processes Element → DOM commit.

questions.title: React Fragments
questions.summary: Fragments group multiple children w/o adding an extra DOM element.
questions.answer: A Fragment groups multiple R^ elements w/o introducing an additional DOM wrapper. Use <>...</> for simple fragments or <Fragment key={...}> for keyed fragments.
questions.underTheHood: R^ represents fragments in its internal tree but does not create a corresponding wrapper DOM element.
pitfalls: Short fragment syntax cannot receive a key.
Fragments do not create DOM nodes.
questions.recall: Fragment → Group children → No extra DOM node.

questions.title: Conditional Rendering
questions.summary: R^ conditionally includes UI using if, ternary, &&, or null.
questions.answer: Conditional r() chooses which elements a C^ returns based on props or state. Common patterns include if statements, ternary expressions, logical &&, and returning null.
questions.underTheHood: Different element types or positions can change C^ identity and cause state reset. R^ reconciles the selected output against the previous tree.
pitfalls: Changing C^ identity can reset state.
Returning null does not prevent the C^ from executing.
followUps: How does conditional r() affect state?
When does R^ remount a C^?
questions.recall: Condition → Element/null → Reconciliation → Preserve or reset state.

questions.title: Rendering Lists & Keys
questions.summary: Lists use map() to produce elements; stable keys help R^ preserve child identity.
questions.answer: R^ renders lists by mapping data into elements. Each sibling should have a stable, unique key that identifies its logical item across updates. Keys help R^ match existing children and preserve state correctly.
questions.underTheHood: During reconciliation, R^ uses element type and key to determine whether an existing Fiber can be reused or must be replaced.
pitfalls: Avoid array index keys for reorderable lists.
Keys are not passed as ordinary props.
questions.recall: List → map() → Stable key → Identity → State preservation.
